The diagram illustrates the process of manufacturing and recycling paper to produce newspapers.
Overall, there are ten main stages involved in the process of producing and reusing paper, beginning with the cutting down of trees and ending with the recycling of old newspapers to make new pulp.
To begin with, trees are cut down and put into a drum to remove the bark. After that, the wood is cut into small chips by a chipper machine.
Next, these wood chippings go into a refiner machine to make pulp.
At the following stage, this pulp is pressed and rolled into big rolls of paper.
In the next part, the rolls of paper are used to print newspapers. When people finish reading them, used newspapers are collected.
Following this, ink is removed from the old newspapers.
In the final step, the paper is made into pulp again and sent back to the pulp pressing step to make new paper.

The diagram illustrates the process of [manufacturing coffee using the dry method].

Overall, there are [12] main stages involved in the process of [producing coffee], beginning with [sorting the coffee beans by hand] and ending with [the packing and selling of the finished products].
At the beginning, the coffee beans are sorted by hand to choose the good one.
After that, they are cleaned using a sieve. In the third step, the beans are spread outside to dry in the sun for about four weeks.
During this time, they are regularly raked and turned so that they dry evenly.
Once dried, the beans are stored in a large silo. Finally, a truck transports them to a mill for further processing.
At the mill, the coffee beans go through hulling to remove their outer skin.
Next, they are graded into different qualities by a flat mesh screen.
After grading, the beans are put into large bags.
At this point, some of the coffee is sold directly in raw form.
The remaining beans are sent to a roasting machine where they are roasted.
In the final step, these roasted beans are packed into bags and sold to customers.
The diagram illustrates the process of [manufacturing olive oil].

Overall, there are [eight] main stages involved in producing [olive oil], beginning with [the harvesting of the olives] and ending with [the transporting of finished products for electricity production].
At the beginning, the olives are collected using a rake.
Following this, the collected olives are stored in a large vat for two to three days.
The olives are washed with cool water to wash before they are crushed by a system which has hammers.
The olive stones then are stored in a container.
The remaining olive paste continues to go through a long tube to filter the process.
In the filter process, the olives undergo a pressing and filtering process by hydraulic to extract the oil.
Then, the liquid is fed into a machine called a centrifuge.
In this process, raw oil is spun to separate it from water and then it is poured into bottles.
Finally, the oil bottles are transported to stores for sales.
The diagram illustrates the process of [manufacturing olive oil].

Overall, there are [eight] main stages involved in the process of [producing olive oil], beginning with [collecting the olives from trees] and ending with [transporting the finished bottles to stores].
First, the olives are collected from trees by a person using a rake. Next, they are stored in a large vat for two to three days.
After that, the olives travel along a conveyor belt where they are washed with cool water.
In the fourth step, a machine with hammers crushes the olives.
This process separates the olive stones, which are stored in a container, while the remaining olive paste moves through a pipe to the next stage.
In the fifth stage, the olive paste is pressed and filtered by a hydraulic press to extract the oil.
Following this, the liquid is sent to a centrifuge machine, where it is spun to separate the oil from the water.
The water is drained away, while the pure oil is poured into bottles.
Finally, the bottled olive oil is loaded onto a truck and transported to stores for sale.
The diagram illustrates the process of [manufacturing cheese from raw milk].

Overall, there are [several] main stages involved in the process of [producing cheese], beginning with [the preparation of raw milk] and ending with [producing either fresh cheese and ripened cheese].
At the beginning, raw milk goes through pasteurization, standardization and filtration for most cheese making, while traditional cheese making skips pasteurization.
After that, the milk is mixed with fermenting microorganisms and rennet in a large tank for coagulation, which separates the liquid into curds and whey. The mixture is then cut, stirred, and cooked.
In the next stage, the whey is drained away, leaving only the curds. Some of these cruds are poured into molds to produce fresh cheese like cottage and cream cheese.
The rest of the curds go through a milling machine, followed by salting on a conveyor belt.
Next, they are placed into molds and pressed to remove additional whey.
Finally, the cheese is stored for ripening to make ripened cheese.
The diagram illustrates stages in the lifespan of [honey bees].
Overall, there are [five] main stages in this process, starting from the [laying of eggs] and finishing with [the maturity of the bees].
The cycle begins when the adult female bee lays an egg. Typically, every three days the females lay from 1 to 2 eggs, which will then hatch between day 9 and day 10.
An immature insect, or a so-called ‘nymph’, makes its appearance.
At the third step of the process, the nymph grows bigger in size and moults for the first time 5 days later, and then the second time on the next 7th day.
The nymph sheds its skin for the last time 9 days after that before emerging to become a young adult honey bee.
It takes 4 days for the young bee to reach the full maturity stage and the process can now be repeated.

To initiate, clay is excavated from the ground using a big digger.
It then passes through a metal grid before moving to a roller where it is mixed with sand and water.
At the following stage, the clay can be moulded into bricks using two methods: placement in a mould or utilization of a wire cutter.
In the fourth phase of the process, the clay bricks are positioned within a drying oven for a duration of one to two days.

Following this, they undergo heating in a kiln, initially at a moderate temperature ranging from 200 to 980 degrees Celcius, then at an elevated temperature of up to 1300 degree Celsius,  preceding a period of two to three days within a cooling chamber.
The final step is that the completed bricks are packaged and transported to point of consumption.

The diagram shows how [plastics are recycled for reuse purposes].

There are [6] main stages involved in the process of [recycling plastics] beginning with [the buying, using and discarding of new plastic products] and ending with [the newly recycled products entering the shop again].
To initiate, new products are purchased, used from shops and thrown away.
At the following stage, plastic bags, along with other garbage, are sent and buried in landfill sites.
Plastic bottles and containers, however, are collected for recycling.
Plastic bottles then are taken to sorting houses where they are divided into different categories.
In the fourth phase of the process, once the plastic has been sorted, it is loaded onto trucks and transported to factories.
Following this, it is processed and made into new plastic products.
The final step is that the recycled plastic products are distributed back to retail shops and the cycle begins all over again.

The diagram shows the process of manufacturing [leather goods].
There are [eleven] main stages involved in the process of [producing leather goods] beginning with [the drying of animal skins] and ending with [the production of various types of leather goods].
To initiate, the hide is hung on a line and dried in the open air before being transported by truck to a factory where it undergoes different cleaning processes.
At the factory, the hide is washed in a mixture of water and lime before being soaked in lime juice.
After that, it is flattened by a special machine and then soaked in tannin, which is a combination of water and vegetable matter.

Moving onto the remaining stages, the hide undergoes a polishing process before being transported by truck to another factory, where it is ready to be used to produce different kinds of products, such as bags, shoes or balls.
The diagrams illustrate how [a modern landfill for household waste is constructed, used and eventually closed].

Overall, the process consists of [three] main stages. First, a large hold is prepared, household waste is then deposited inside. Finally, the hole is sealed, and the gases are released through a separate pipe.
During construction, a deep man-made hole is excavated in an area of natural rock.
The inside of this space is covered first with a layer of clay and then synthetic lining, which prevents waste liquid from entering the surrounding area.
A series of drainage pipes is installed along the bottom and connected to a drainage tank.
When the landfill is in use, trucks deposit household waste into the prepared hole.
As the waste accumulates, liquid produced inside flows downwards and enters the drainage pipes. It is then carried into the tank at the base of the landfill.
In the final stage, the filled landfill is covered with a thick layer of clay.
A vertical pipeline is also installed through the waste so that gases can escape safely after the site has been closed.
The diagram shows the process of [manufacturing chocolate].
There are [nine] main stages involved in the process of [producing chocolate] beginning with [the harvesting of ripe red pods] and ending with [the creation of finished chocolate bars].
To initiate, white cacao beans are extracted from the ripe red pods that grow on cacao trees.
These white beans are then placed in containers to undergo fermentation for a period ranging from 2 to 10 days.
Following this, the fermented beans are spread out in the sun to dry thoroughly.
Once dried, they are roasted in an oven at temperatures between 120 and 150 degrees Celsius.
Moving onto the remaining stages, the roasted beans are crushed in a machine to remove their outer shells, leaving only the inner parts.
Afterwards, these inner parts are subjected to a process called conching, where they are pressed to produce a liquid mixture.
The resulting liquid then undergoes tempering, which involves heating and cooling to stabilize the texture.
Finally, the liquid chocolate is poured into molds and cooled to form solid chocolate bars ready for consumption.
The diagram illustrates the components of [a hot air balloon] and its mechanics.
The diagram illustrates the structure and the operation of a [hot air balloon].

Overall, it is clear that a hot air balloon is made up of two main sections: the upper envelope and the lower basket assembly. Additionally, its operation relies on burning propane to heat the air inside the balloon, which generates the necessary lift to fly and allows the pilot to control its altitude.
In terms of structure, the bottom part of the hot air balloon consists of a basket equipped with two propane cylinders, above which a burner is positioned.
This entire lower assembly is connected to the skirt—the lower opening of the balloon—via strong ropes.
The main body of the balloon is the envelope, which is constructed from multiple gores, each made up of smaller panels.
At the very top of the envelope lies a parachute valve, a self-sealing flap that can be opened or closed.
Regarding its operation, the flight process begins when propane from the cylinders is mixed with air in the burner, igniting a flame that heats the surrounding air.

This heated air is directed into the envelope, filling it completely. Since hot air is lighter and less dense than the cooler surrounding air, it creates an upward lift that causes the balloon to rise.
To control the flight, the pilot uses the parachute valve to manage the amount of hot air escaping from the top, thereby regulating the balloon's altitude.
The diagram describes the process of [making bamboo fabric].
There are [nine] main stages involved in the process of [producing bamboo fabric], beginning with [planting bamboo plants] and ending with [making clothing items].
To begin with, bamboo plants are planted in spring and then harvested in autumn.
After harvesting, the bamboo is cut into strips using a circular saw. Next, these strips are crushed into a liquid pulp.
At the following stages, the pulp is filtered to separate long fibres from the liquid.
In the next part, the fibres are softened by adding water and amine oxide.
Following this, they are spun into balls of yarn. The yarn is then woven to make a bamboo fabric.
In the final step, this fabric is used to produce finished products such as socks and clothes.

he harvested stalks are then sliced into narrow strips by a circular saw before being mechanically crushed to form a liquid pulp.

The process continues with the chemical treatment stages, where water and amine oxide are introduced to soften the extracted fibres.
Once softened, these fibres are spun into balls of yarn.
In the penultimate step, the yarn is woven into sheets of bamboo fabrics.
Ultimately, this material is tailored into various apparel items, including socks and clothes.
The diagram illustrates how [ethanol is produced as a biofuel and how it is used].

Overall, there are [several] main stages involved in [the cyclical process of producing ethanol] beginning with [the growth of plants] and ending with [vehicles releasing carbon dioxide, which helps new plants grow].
In the first stage, plants and trees absorb energy from sunlight and carbon dioxide to grow.
After they are fully grown, these crops are harvested by a tractor.
Next, the harvested plants are put into a machine for pre-processing to produce cellulose.
Following this, the cellulose is sent to a factory for a processing stage where it is converted into sugars.
In the next step, microbes are added to the sugars to produce ethanol. Once the ethanol is ready, it is used as fuel for different vehicles, such as cars, trucks, and airplanes.
Finally, when these vehicles run, they release carbon dioxide back into the air.
This gas is then absorbed again by plants and trees, repeating the whole process.
The flow chart illustrates the sequential stages involved in the production of ethanol biofuel and its cyclical consumption by transport vehicles.

Overall, the process operates as a closed-loop system, commencing with the biological growth of vegetation, proceeding through chemical extraction and fermentation, and culminating in the emission of carbon dioxide that is reabsorbed by plants.
Initially, plants and trees utilize solar energy and atmospheric carbon dioxide to develop.
Once mature, the vegetation is harvested mechanically using agricultural machinery.
The harvested biomass then undergoes a pre-processing stage, where it is broken down into cellulose.
Subsequently, this cellulose is transported to a processing facility where it is converted into sugars through chemical treatment.
In the subsequent phase, microbes are introduced to ferment the sugars, resulting in the creation of liquid ethanol.
This refined biofuel is then supplied to various models of transportation, including passenger cars, trucks, and airplanes.
As these vehicles consume the fuel, their engines emit carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere.
Ultimately, this emitted gas acts as a vital input for growing plants, thereby completing an endless ecological cycle.
The diagram shows the process of [manufacturing carbonated drinks].

Overall, there are [five] main stages involved in the process of [producing carbonated drinks] beginning with [the cleaning of water] and ending with [completely products delivered to the supermarket].
In the first stage, raw water undergoes a cleaning process to clean from filtering, softening, and adding chemicals.
After completely cleaning, it is pumped into electric heaters.
Processed water is then cooled through a pipe before being introduced in a modern device which sends out carbon dioxide.
The output of the device is carbonated water.
The carbonated water is then transferred to the mixing tank and is combined with chemicals including colouring, syrup and flavour.
Following this, it is filtered and poured into bottles or cans.
Finally, the bottles or cans are packaged in cartons and sent to the supermarket.

Overall, there are five main stages involved in the process of producing carbonated drinks, beginning with water cleaning and ending with packaging and delivering finished drinks to supermarkets.
In the first stage, raw water goes through a filter, a water softener, and chemicals to be cleaned.
In the second stage, the water is pumped into electric heaters and then cooled through a pipe.
After cooling, carbon dioxide is added to the water in a chamber to produce carbonated water.
In the third stage, this carbonated water is moved into a mixing tank, where it is mixed with colouring, syrup, and flavour.
Following this, in stage 4, the liquid is filtered again and poured into bottles and cans.
Finally, in the packaging stage, the bottles and cans are packed into cardboard boxes and transported to supermarkets by truck.
The diagram illustrates the linear process by which carbonated soft drinks are produced.

Overall, the production comprises five distinct stages, commencing with water purification and carbonation, followed by flavor blending, and culminating in bottling, package, and supermarket distribution.
In the initial stage, raw water undergoes purification by passing through a filter, a water softener, and chemical treatment.
During the second stage, the purified water is pumped into electric heaters before being cooled as it travels through a cooling pipe.
It then enters a carbonation chamber where carbon dioxide is injected to form carbonated water.
In the subsequent stage, the carbonated liquid is transferred to a large mixing tank, where it is blended with colouring, syrup, and flavourings.
Once the mixture is complete, stage 4 involves filtering the drink once more before it is filled into bottles and cans.
In the final phase, these packaged containers are boxed into cartons and dispatched by truck to supermarkets for sale.
The diagram illustrates the life cycle of [the salmon fish].
Overall, this is [a natural cycle] consisting of [seven] main stages, starting from [eggs in fresh water] and ending with [salmon laying eggs and dying].
First, the eggs are laid in fresh water and take about three months to hatch. In the next stage, the baby fish are called alevin, and they feed on a yolk-sac for several weeks.
After that, they grow into fry at 5 to 10 weeks old and begin to swim. In the fourth stage, when the fish are several months old, they become parr and develop finger-like markings on their bodies.
Next, between 1 and 3 years old, the fish turn into smolt. At this time, they gather into groups and swim out to the sea.
The smolt then grows into adult fish, spending 1 to 8 years living in the ocean.
Finally, the adult salmon return to fresh water to spawn, and they die within two weeks after laying new eggs, starting the cycle again.
The diagram depicts the cyclical life cycle of a salmon, detailing its development from eggs to maturity.

Overall, the process represents a closed-loop biological cycle comprising seven distinct phases. The first begins life in a freshwater habitat, migrates to the marine environment as it matures, and eventually returns to fresh water to reproduce and die.
Initially, salmon eggs are deposited in freshwater environments and hatch after approximately three months.
The emerging hatchlings, termed alevin, survive by absorbing nutrients from their attached yolk-sac for a few weeks.
Following this, they transition into the “fry” stage at 5 to 10 weeks of age, when they become capable of independent swimming.
Over the subsequent months, they develop distinctive vertical “finger” stripes on their scales, entering the “parr” phase.
Between 1 and 3 years of age, the fish transform into smolt, grouping together before migrating towards the open sea.
Once in the marine habitat, they mature into adult salmon and reside there for a period ranging from 1 to 8 years.
Ultimately, mature spawning adults migrate back upstream to freshwater areas to lay eggs, culminating in their death within two weeks, which allows the life cycle to recommence.
